activity_context.topic_title: Calculating Limits of Radical Functions Using Conjugate Multiplication

feedback.worked_solution:
If we attempt to evaluate the limit, we get an indeterminate form:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {8}^{+}}\frac{\sqrt{x+1}-3}{x-8} & =\frac{\sqrt{8+1}-3}{8-8}=\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we need to first simplify the limit. Since the radical is in the numerator, we can multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the numerator. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {8}^{+}}\frac{\sqrt{x+1}-3}{x-8} & ={lim}_{x\to {8}^{+}}\frac{(\sqrt{x+1}-3)(\sqrt{x+1}+3)}{(x-8)(\sqrt{x+1}+3)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {8}^{+}}\frac{{(\sqrt{x+1})}^{2}-{3}^{2}}{(x-8)(\sqrt{x+1}+3)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {8}^{+}}\frac{x+1-9}{(x-8)(\sqrt{x+1}+3)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {8}^{+}}\frac{x-8}{(x-8)(\sqrt{x+1}+3)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to {8}^{+}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{x+1}+3} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{8+1}+3} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$
